blocks.text:
Biot Savart Law : With the help of experimental results, Biot and Savart arrived at a mathematical expression that gives the magnetic field at some point in space in terms of the current that produces the field.

BIOT SAVART LAW  :

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{dB}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{id} \ell \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^2}\\ &\text { (here } \frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi}=10^{-7} \frac{\mathrm{~T}-\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{~A}} \text { ) } \end{aligned}$

$\mu_0: \text { Permeability of free space }$

$\mu: \text { Permeability of a medium }$

$\mu_r: \text { Relative Permeability of a medium }$

$\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \quad \text { where } \mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \frac{\mathrm{Tm}}{\mathrm{~A}}$

Biot Savarts Law in Vector Form:

$\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \dfrac{\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{~d} \vec{\ell} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

Direction of Magnetic Field :-

Right Hand Palm Rule

Thumb: along the direction of current

Fingers: along the direction of point where B is to be found

Palm: indicates direction of magnetic field

Case I :– Wire is in the plane of the paper :-

Case II :– Wire is perpendicular to the plane of the paper :-

Note: For a straight current carrying wire M.F. lines are in form of concentric circles.

Magnetic Field due to Moving Charge

$\begin{aligned} &\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3}\\ &\text { (in vector form) } \end{aligned}$ $\rightarrow$  Charge will be written with Sign

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{qv} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^2} \\ & \text { (in scalar form) } \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:

Magnetic Field due to Circular Coil :

$\text { For single loop : - } B_0=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}$

$\text { For } \mathrm{N} \text { loops: - } \mathrm{B}_0=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{NI}}{2 \mathrm{R}}$

Magnetic Field due to Circular Arc :

$\mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{I} \alpha}{\mathrm{R}}$

NOTE: $\alpha$ must be in radian only

(1) Wire of circuit loop is uniform:

Magnetic field produced by both the arc is at the centre of the circuit loop is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. (Unit should be uniform)

$\text { So }\left(B_0\right)_{\text {net }}=0 $ (always and it is free from angle of connection of terminals)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Ampere Circuital Law:

Line integral of magnetic field along any closed loop is equal to $μ_0 $ times the net current crossing the surface bounded by the loop.

$\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~d} \ell}=\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{enc}}$

Note:

It is applicable only for steady/constant current

Magnetic Field due to Long Thick wire

A : Outside the wire surface

$B_{\text {out }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}, B_{\text {out }} \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$

B : On the wire surface

$B_{\text {sur }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi R}$

C : Inside the wire surface

$B_{\text {in }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi R^2} r, B_{\text {in }} \propto r$

Note: Magnetic field is maximum at the surface of wire.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic field due to Solenoid :

• Magnetic field is produced along axis of solenoid. Outside a long solenoid,(Equitorial  Points) magnetic field is almost Zero.

Magnetic Field Inside a Long Solenoid :

$B=\mu_0 n i$

For a long solenoid length of solenoid is very large as compared to radius of solenoid i.e. $l>>r$

Magnetic Field due to Long Solenoid :

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{B}_0=\mu_0 \mathrm{nI} \quad \mathrm{~B}_0=\mu_0\left(\frac{\mathrm{~N}}{\ell}\right) \mathrm{I} \end{aligned}$

$\text { M.F. outside the solenoid } \quad B=0$

$\text { M.F. at the edges/end points } \quad B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}}{2}$

$\text { In presence of Core, } \mu \rightarrow \mu_0 \mu_r$

Magnetic Field due to Finite Length Solenoid :

$\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}}{2}\left(\sin \phi_1+\sin \phi_2\right) \quad  n=\frac{N}{l} \text { (turn density or turns/meter) }$

Note: Magnetic Field produced by a solenoid resembles the Magnetic field of a Bar Magnet. So, a solenoid acts as a Magnetic Dipole and is used as electromagnet in many devices.

Magnetic field due to Toroid: A toroid can be considered as a ring-shaped closed solenoid also called endless solenoid. Toroid is a solenoid bent in ring shape.

Point A: Magnetic field in the empty space surrounded by

$\text { toroid }\left(\mathrm{r}<\mathrm{R}_1\right)$

$\begin{aligned}  & \mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \frac{\mathrm{~N}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~B}=\mu_{\mathrm{o}} \mathrm{nI} \end{aligned}$

If r is not given then for magnetic field inside the toroid

$\mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{m}}}$

$\left[\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}{2}=\text { mean radius of toroid }\right]$

blocks.title: Points To Remember
blocks.text:
Key Note

• Magnetic field of toroid is non-uniform because at each point direction of magnetic field is not same.

• It is not a Magnetic Dipole.

• Magnetic field produced by a toroid is directed along its circular axis and constant in magnitude over its entire cross section.

• Magnetic field at the centre of toroid is always zero.

modules.name: Motion of Charge in Magnetic Field

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic Force on Moving Charge: Consider a charge q moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in uniform magnetic field  $\vec{B}$ such that $\vec{v}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with  $\vec{B}$ then magnetic force experienced by the charge is given by

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ & \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{qvB} \sin \theta \end{aligned}$

$\text { Case-1: } \theta=0^{\circ} \text { or } 180^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{F}=0$

$\text { Case-2: } \theta=90^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\max }=\mathrm{qvB}$

$\left(\theta \text { can vary from } 0^{\circ} \text { to } 180^{\circ}\right)$

Motion of Charged Particle in Uniform Magnetic Field:

Based on angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$, charge can move on three type of paths in Uniform Magnetic Field

Case 1

$\begin{aligned} &\theta=0^{\circ} / 180^{\circ}\\ &\text { Straight Line Path } \end{aligned}$

Case 2: Motion of charge particle in uniform transverse magnetic field

$\begin{aligned} &\theta=90^{\circ}\\ &\text { Circular Path } \end{aligned}$

(a) Radius of circular path :

$\mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}}, \text { where } \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{mv}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mE}_{\mathrm{K}}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}_{\mathrm{acc}}}$

(b) Time period :  $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}}$

Note:

  • Time period does not depend on velocity or Radius.
Case 3: Motion of Charge Particle in Oblique Magnetic Field $\left(\theta \neq 0^{\circ}, \mathbf{9 0}^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}\right)$

Axis of helix: It is a straight line along external magnetic field which joins all the centres of circular turns, called axis of helix.

(a) Radius of helical path : $r=\frac{m v \sin \theta}{q B} \quad \text{ OR } \quad  r=\frac{m V_{\perp}}{q B}$

(b) Time period : $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}}$

(c) Pitch of helix :The linear distance travelled by the charge particle in one revolution or in one time period along external magnetic field direction is called 'pitch of helix'.

$\mathrm{p}=(\mathrm{v} \cos \theta) \mathrm{T}$

$\text { where } \mathrm{T}=\displaystyle \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{p}=\displaystyle \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{mv} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{qB}}$

$$Lorentz Force: When a charge is moving in a region, where both electric field E and magnetic field B exist, then electric and magnetic forces are acting on it. The resultant of these forces called electromagnetic or Lorentz force on charge. (zero gravity).

Net Electromagnetic force is known as Lorentz force.

modules.name: Magnetic Force on a Current Carrying Wire

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Current Carrying wire in Uniform Magnetic Field : When a current carrying conductor placed in magnetic field, a magnetic force exerts on each free electron which are present inside the conductor. The resultant of these forces on all the free electrons is called magnetic force on conductor.

Net force on wire due to all such current elements

$\vec{F}=I(\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$

If B is uniform,

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{I}\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~L}}_{\mathrm{eff}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}\right)$

$L_{\text {eff }}$ is the displacement vector from starting point of current to end point of current.

Direction of magnetic force :

Magnetic force on the wire we can find by Right Hand Palm Rule

Magnetic Force Between Two Parallel Current Carrying Wires :

Definition of Ampere

Magnetic force/unit length for both infinite length conductor gives as

$\mathrm{f}=\dfrac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_1 \mathrm{I}_2}{2 \pi \mathrm{~d}}=\dfrac{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right)(1)(1)}{2 \pi(1)}=2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$

'Ampere' is the current which, when passed through each of two parallel infinite long straight conductors placed in free space at a distance of 1 m from each other, produces between them a force  $2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Bar Magnet: It is made up of iron, steel or any other ferromagnetic substance or ferromagnetic composite, having permanent magnetic properties. Two poles are present in a Bar magnet, North Pole and South Pole.

Properties of bar magnets:

1. When a bar magnet is suspended freely near the surface of the earth, it tends to align always in the nearly North-South direction. One end of the bar magnet always pointing towards the geographic North is called the North pole of the magnet. The other end that always point towards the geographic South is called the South pole of the magnet.

2. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract each other.

3. The North and South poles of a bar magnet cannot be separated. The magnetic monopoles do not exist.

4. Bar magnets are made up of ferromagnetic materials, like iron, cobalt, nickel etc.

5. The magnetic field lines outside a bar magnet move from north pole to south pole.

6. The magnetic field lines inside a bar magnet move from south pole to north pole.

A magnetic dipole consists of a pair of magnetic poles of equal and opposite strength separated by small distance.

Dipole Moment of a bar magnet: The magnetic dipole moment of a bar magnet is defined as a vector quantity having magnitude equal to the

product of pole strength (m) with effective length ($l$ ) and directed along the axis of the magnet from south pole to north pole.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{m} \vec{\ell}$$$

Where

m: Pole Strength (Unit: A-m)

$\ell$ : effective distance between the North pole and South Pole

M: Dipole Moment of bar magnet

Pole strength (m) of each pole $\propto$ area of the cross-section for a given bar magnet.

Magnetic Moment of Current Carrying Coil (Loop) :

Current carrying coil (or loop) behaves like magnetic dipole. The face of coil in which current appears to flow anticlockwise acts as north pole while face of coil in which current appears to flow clockwise acts as south pole.

A current-carrying coil acts as a Magnetic Dipole.

$\text { ACW } \rightarrow \text { North Pole } \quad \text { CW } \rightarrow \text { South Pole }$

For a coil of turns 'N', geometrical area 'A', carries a current 'I'

Magnetic Moment,  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}=\mathrm{NI} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}}$

where $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}}$ is area vector perpendicular to the plane of the coil and along its axis.

SI unit :  $\mathrm{A}-\mathrm{m}^2 \text { or } \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{T}$

The direction of $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}$ can be found out by right hand thumb rule.

modules.name: Torque and Potential Energy of Magnetic DIipole

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Torque on a Magnetic Dipole in Uniform Magnetic Field:

(a) Bar magnet

Consider a bar magnet of magnetic moment  $\vec{M}$  held in a uniform magnetic field $\vec(B)$ making an angle  $\theta$ with the field. Then the magnet experiences a torque given by

Torque = force × perpendicular distance between force couple

$\begin{aligned} \tau & =\mathrm{MB} \sin \theta, \text { where } \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m} \ell \\ \vec{\tau} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \end{aligned}$

$\tau=\mathrm{MB} \sin \theta$

(b) Coil or Loop : If a loop carries a current of magnitude $I$ and magnetic moment $\vec{M}$ held in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ making an angle $\theta$

Then the loop experiences a torque given by,

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}  \end{aligned}$

If loop have N turns then

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\mathrm{NI}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ \tau & =\mathrm{NIAB} \sin \theta \end{aligned} \quad  \text { where } \vec{M}=N I \vec{A}$

Note:

• Tendency of torque on dipole is try to align the $\vec{M}$ in the direction of  $\vec{B}$ or tries to makes the axis of dipole parallel to $\vec{B}$ or makes the plane of coil (or loop) perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.

Work Done in Rotating the Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field:

When a bar magnet or coil of dipole moment M is kept in a uniform magnetic field B it experiences a torque which tries to align it in the direction of external magnetic field B . Work has to be done in rotation the magnet or coil.

$\begin{aligned}  & \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{MB}\left(\cos \theta_1-\cos \theta_2\right) \end{aligned}$

Potential Energy of the Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field: The potential energy of dipole defined as work done in rotating the dipole from a direction perpendicular to the given direction.

$\text { Work done in rotating the dipole from } \theta_1=90^{\circ} \text { to } \theta_2=0^{\circ}$

$\begin{aligned} &$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{MB}\left(\cos 90^{\circ}-\cos \theta\right) \\ & \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{MB} \cos \theta \end{aligned}$$\\ &\text { In vector form } U=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}} \end{aligned}$$

blocks.title: Potential Energy of the Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field(Special Cases)

rows: $\text { When } \vec{M} \text { and } \vec{B} \text { are parallel }$\theta=0^{\circ}$\tau=0$$\mathrm{U}_{\min }=-\mathrm{MB}$The dipole has minimum potential energy and it is in stable equilibrium.

$\text { When } \vec{M} \text { and } \vec{B} \text { are perpendicular }$ $\begin{gathered} \theta=90^{\circ} \\ \tau=\mathrm{MB} \\ \mathrm{U}=0 \end{gathered}$$\text { No Equilibrium as } \tau \neq 0$

$\text { When } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \text { and } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \text { are anti-parallel }$$\begin{gathered} \theta=180^{\circ} \\ \tau=0 \\ \mathrm{U}_{\max }=\mathrm{MB} \end{gathered}$The dipole has maximum potential energy and it is in unstable equilibrium.

Moving Coil Galvanometer:

Construction: The galvanometer consists of a coil, with many turns, free to rotate about a fixed axis, in a uniform radial magnetic field. There is a cylindrical soft iron core which not only makes the field radial but also increases the strength of the magnetic field. A spiral spring is also attached to the coil which resists the rotation of coil.

Working Principle: When a current carrying coil is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a torque

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\operatorname{NI}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ \tau & =\operatorname{NIAB} \sin \theta \\ \tau & =\operatorname{NIAB} \end{aligned}$

$\left(\theta=90^{\circ} \text { due to radial magnetic field }\right)$

This torque tends to rotate the coil by $ \phi$ angle.

The spring S provides a counter torque $ \mathrm{C} \phi$ that balances the magnetic torque. In equilibrium,

$\mathrm{C} \phi=\mathrm{NIAB} \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{NAB}} \phi$

$I \propto \phi$

Current Sensitivity: Current sensitivity is defined as the deflection produced in the galvanometer when a unit current flows through it.

$\text { C.S. }=\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{N A B}{C}(\operatorname{rad} / A) $

Voltage Sensitivity :Voltage sensitivity is equal to the deflection per unit voltage applied across the voltmeter.

$\text { V.S. }=\frac{\phi}{V}=\frac{\phi}{I R}=\frac{N A B}{C R}(\mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{V})$

Atomic Magnetism: Consider an electron revolving around a nucleus in an atom. Due to the motion of the electrons, the orbit behaves like a current-carrying loop. Due to this, the magnetic field is produced at the centre of the orbit. This is called 'atomic magnetism'.

(a) Effective current

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{~T}}=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{~T}}=\mathrm{ef}=\frac{\mathrm{e} \omega}{2 \pi}=\frac{\mathrm{ev}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \\ & \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{qv}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \text { (In general) } \end{aligned}$

(b) Induced Magnetic Field at the center

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{B}_{\text{in}} &= \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r} = \frac{\mu_0 e}{2 T r} = \frac{\mu_0 e f}{2 r} = \frac{\mu_0}{2 r} \left( \frac{e v}{2 \pi r} \right) \\ &= \frac{\mu_0 e v}{4 \pi r^2} \\ \mathrm{B}_{\text{in}} &= \frac{\mu_0 q v}{4 \pi r^2} \quad \text{(In general)} \end{aligned}$

(c) Magnetic Moment

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{IA}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{ev}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}\right) \pi \mathrm{r}^2=\frac{\mathrm{e} \omega \mathrm{r}^2}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{evr}}{2} \\ & \mathrm{M}=\frac{\mathrm{qvr}}{2}(\text { In general }) \end{aligned}$

NOTE: The ratio of magnetic moment to angular momentum, called the gyromagnetic ratio of a uniform rotating object which is charged uniformly, is always a constant and equal to half of the specific charge. Irrespective of the shape of the conductor M/L=q/2m

The magnetic field at axial point (or End-on position) of dipole:  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

The magnetic field at equatorial position (Broad-side on position) of dipole:  $\vec{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{(-\vec{M})}{r^3}$

Angular SHM of magnetic dipole:

When a dipole is suspended in a uniform magnetic field it will align itself parallel to field. Now if it is given a small angular displacement $\theta$ with respect to its equilibrium position. The restoring torque acts on it :

$\mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{MB}}} \quad \text { where } \mathrm{I}: \text { Moment of Inertia }=\frac{\mathrm{ml}^2}{12}\{\mathrm{~m} \text { : mass of magnet, } \ell: \text { length of magnet }\}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetizing field or Magnetic Intensity (H) : Field in which a material is placed for magnetization, called as magnetizing field.

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{o}}} \\ & \text { unit of } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}}: \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{m} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}_{\mathrm{o}}: \text { Magnetic Field } \\ & \mu_0: \text { Permeability of free space } \end{aligned}$

$\text { Intensity of magnetization ( } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}} \text { ) }$: When a magnetic material is placed in magnetising field then induced dipole moment per unit volume of that material is known as intensity of magnetisation.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{~V}}$

$\text { unit of } \vec{I}: A / m \quad\left\{\because \frac{\vec{M}}{V}=\frac{I \vec{A}}{V}=\frac{\text { ampere } \times \text { meter }^2}{\text { meter }^3}\right\}$

Induced magnetic field due to these induced dipoles in the material is given by:

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mu_{\mathrm{o}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}$

Magnetic susceptibility  $\left(\chi_m\right)$ :

$\chi_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{H}}$ [It is a scalar with no units & dimensions].

Physically it represents the ease with which a magnetic material can be magnetised.

Note: A material with more $\chi_{\mathrm{m}}$ can be changed into a magnet easily.

Magnetic Permeability $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ :

It represents the degree up to which a material can be penetrated by the magnetic field lines.

$\text { Relative Permeability ( } \mu_r \text { ) }$:

$\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0}$

It has no units and dimensions.

$\text { Relation between } \mu \text { and } \chi_{\mathrm{m}}$ :

When a magnetic material is placed in a magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}$  for magnetization, then total magnetic field in the material is

$\begin{aligned} & \mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\left(1+\chi_{\mathrm{m}}\right) \end{aligned}$

For vacuum, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0$

For air, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1.04, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0.04$

Magnetic Hysteresis: Only Ferromagnetic materials show magnetic hysteresis, when Ferromagnetic material is placed in external magnetic field for magnetization.

  • Magnetizing Field Increase: As the magnetizing field increases, the magnetic field inside the material also increases.
  • Saturation: At a certain point, further increase in the magnetizing field causes no change in the magnetic field inside (saturation).
  • Decrease in Magnetizing Field: When the magnetizing field is reduced, the magnetic field inside decreases (A to B).
  • Retentivity: After removing the magnetizing field, a residual magnetic field remains in the material $\text { (known as Retentivity, } B_r \text { ). }$
  • Coercivity: To remove the residual magnetic field, an external field is applied in the opposite direction until the net magnetic field is zero (B to C). The field strength required to do this is called Coercivity $\left(H_c\right)$
  • Reversal of Magnetization: As the magnetizing field is increased further, the magnetic field inside the material starts rising again (C to D).
  • Cycle Repeats: The curve repeats as the magnetizing field is decreased and reversed, showing hysteresis (lagging of B behind H).
  • Hysteresis Curve: The lag of B behind H forms the hysteresis curve.
Cause of hysteresis: By removing external magnetizing field (H = 0), the magnetic moment of some domains remains aligned in the applied direction of previous magnetizing field which results into a residual magnetism.

Hysteresis Loss:

• The area of the hysteresis loop is equal to the energy loss per cycle per unit volume.
    • Its value is different for different materials.
    • The work done per cycle per unit volume of material is equal to the area of the hysteresis loop.

$\text { Total energy loss in material }=\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}$

$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\text { volume of material } \times \text { area of hysteresis curve } \times \text { frequency } \times \text { time. }$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t} \text { joule } \\ & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{~J}} \text { calorie } \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Biot Savart Law : With the help of experimental results, Biot and Savart arrived at a mathematical expression that gives the magnetic field at some point in space in terms of the current that produces the field.

BIOT SAVART LAW  :

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{dB}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{id} \ell \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^2}\\ &\text { (here } \frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi}=10^{-7} \frac{\mathrm{~T}-\mathrm{m}}{\mathrm{~A}} \text { ) } \end{aligned}$

$\mu_0: \text { Permeability of free space }$

$\mu: \text { Permeability of a medium }$

$\mu_r: \text { Relative Permeability of a medium }$

$\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\frac{\mu}{\mu_0} \quad \text { where } \mu_0=4 \pi \times 10^{-7} \frac{\mathrm{Tm}}{\mathrm{~A}}$

Biot Savarts Law in Vector Form:

$\mathrm{d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}=\dfrac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \dfrac{\mathrm{i}(\mathrm{~d} \vec{\ell} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

Direction of Magnetic Field :-

Right Hand Palm Rule

Thumb: along the direction of current

Fingers: along the direction of point where B is to be found

Palm: indicates direction of magnetic field

Case I :– Wire is in the plane of the paper :-

Case II :– Wire is perpendicular to the plane of the paper :-

Note: For a straight current carrying wire M.F. lines are in form of concentric circles.

Magnetic Field due to Moving Charge

$\begin{aligned} &\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{r}})}{\mathrm{r}^3}\\ &\text { (in vector form) } \end{aligned}$ $\rightarrow$  Charge will be written with Sign

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{qv} \sin \theta}{\mathrm{r}^2} \\ & \text { (in scalar form) } \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core concepts
blocks.text:
Application of Biot-Savart Law :

(1) Magnetic Field due to Thin Wire of Finite Length :

$\mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}\left(\sin \phi_1+\sin \phi_2\right)$

(2 )Magnetic Field due to Infinite Straight Wire :

$\Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}(1+1)=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}(2) \Rightarrow \mathrm{B}_{\infty}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{2 \pi \mathrm{a}}$

(3) Magnetic Field due to Semi Infinite Straight Wire :

Case-1

$\phi_1 \rightarrow 90^{\circ}$

$\phi_2=0^{\circ}$

$B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}\left(\sin 90^{\circ}+\sin 0^{\circ}\right) \Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}} \otimes$

Case-2

$\phi_1 \rightarrow 90^{\circ}$

$\phi_2=\theta$

$B=\frac{\mu_0 I}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}\left(\sin 90^{\circ}+\sin \theta\right) \Rightarrow B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}}{4 \pi \mathrm{a}}(1+\sin \theta) \otimes$

blocks.text:
• Curl the fingers of right hand in the direction of current in the loop then thumb will indicated the direction of magnetic field

Magnetic Field due to Circular Coil :

$\text { For single loop : - } B_0=\frac{\mu_0 I}{2 R}$

$\text { For } \mathrm{N} \text { loops: - } \mathrm{B}_0=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{NI}}{2 \mathrm{R}}$

Magnetic Field due to Circular Arc :

$\mathrm{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{\mathrm{I} \alpha}{\mathrm{R}}$

NOTE: $\alpha$ must be in radian only

(1) Wire of circuit loop is uniform:

Magnetic field produced by both the arc is at the centre of the circuit loop is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. (Unit should be uniform)

$\text { So }\left(B_0\right)_{\text {net }}=0 $ (always and it is free from angle of connection of terminals)

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic Field at the Axis of Circular loop

$B_P=\dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2\left(R^2+x^2\right)^{3 / 2}}=\dfrac{B_0}{\left(1+\dfrac{x^2}{R^2}\right)^{3 / 2}}$

Case 1 : At very large distance from centre

$\Rightarrow B \approx \dfrac{\mu_0 I R^2}{2 x^3}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Ampere Circuital Law:

Line integral of magnetic field along any closed loop is equal to $μ_0 $ times the net current crossing the surface bounded by the loop.

$\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~d} \ell}=\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{enc}}$

Note:

It is applicable only for steady/constant current

Magnetic Field due to Long Thick wire

A : Outside the wire surface

$B_{\text {out }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi r}, B_{\text {out }} \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$

B : On the wire surface

$B_{\text {sur }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi R}$

C : Inside the wire surface

$B_{\text {in }}=\dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2 \pi R^2} r, B_{\text {in }} \propto r$

Note: Magnetic field is maximum at the surface of wire.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic field due to Solenoid :

• Magnetic field is produced along axis of solenoid. Outside a long solenoid,(Equitorial  Points) magnetic field is almost Zero.

Magnetic Field Inside a Long Solenoid :

$B=\mu_0 n i$

For a long solenoid length of solenoid is very large as compared to radius of solenoid i.e. $l>>r$

Magnetic Field due to Long Solenoid :

$\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{B}_0=\mu_0 \mathrm{nI} \quad \mathrm{~B}_0=\mu_0\left(\frac{\mathrm{~N}}{\ell}\right) \mathrm{I} \end{aligned}$

$\text { M.F. outside the solenoid } \quad B=0$

$\text { M.F. at the edges/end points } \quad B=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}}{2}$

$\text { In presence of Core, } \mu \rightarrow \mu_0 \mu_r$

Magnetic Field due to Finite Length Solenoid :

$\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{P}}=\frac{\mu_0 \mathrm{nI}}{2}\left(\sin \phi_1+\sin \phi_2\right) \quad  n=\frac{N}{l} \text { (turn density or turns/meter) }$

Note: Magnetic Field produced by a solenoid resembles the Magnetic field of a Bar Magnet. So, a solenoid acts as a Magnetic Dipole and is used as electromagnet in many devices.

Magnetic field due to Toroid: A toroid can be considered as a ring-shaped closed solenoid also called endless solenoid. Toroid is a solenoid bent in ring shape.

Point A: Magnetic field in the empty space surrounded by

$\text { toroid }\left(\mathrm{r}<\mathrm{R}_1\right)$

$\begin{aligned}  & \mathrm{B}=\mu_0 \frac{\mathrm{~N}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \mathrm{I} \\ & \mathrm{~B}=\mu_{\mathrm{o}} \mathrm{nI} \end{aligned}$

If r is not given then for magnetic field inside the toroid

$\mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{N}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{m}}}$

$\left[\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{R}_1+\mathrm{R}_2}{2}=\text { mean radius of toroid }\right]$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetic Force on Moving Charge: Consider a charge q moving with velocity $\vec{v}$ in uniform magnetic field  $\vec{B}$ such that $\vec{v}$ makes an angle $\theta$ with  $\vec{B}$ then magnetic force experienced by the charge is given by

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{q}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{v}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ & \mathrm{F}=\mathrm{qvB} \sin \theta \end{aligned}$

$\text { Case-1: } \theta=0^{\circ} \text { or } 180^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{F}=0$

$\text { Case-2: } \theta=90^{\circ}$

$\Rightarrow \mathrm{F}_{\max }=\mathrm{qvB}$

$\left(\theta \text { can vary from } 0^{\circ} \text { to } 180^{\circ}\right)$

Motion of Charged Particle in Uniform Magnetic Field:

Based on angle between $\vec{v}$ and $\vec{B}$, charge can move on three type of paths in Uniform Magnetic Field

Case 1

$\begin{aligned} &\theta=0^{\circ} / 180^{\circ}\\ &\text { Straight Line Path } \end{aligned}$

Case 2: Motion of charge particle in uniform transverse magnetic field

$\begin{aligned} &\theta=90^{\circ}\\ &\text { Circular Path } \end{aligned}$

(a) Radius of circular path :

$\mathrm{r}=\frac{\mathrm{mv}}{\mathrm{qB}}, \text { where } \mathrm{P}=\mathrm{mv}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mE}_{\mathrm{K}}}=\sqrt{2 \mathrm{mqV}_{\mathrm{acc}}}$

(b) Time period :  $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}}$

Note:

  • Time period does not depend on velocity or Radius.
Case 3: Motion of Charge Particle in Oblique Magnetic Field $\left(\theta \neq 0^{\circ}, \mathbf{9 0}^{\circ}, 180^{\circ}\right)$

Axis of helix: It is a straight line along external magnetic field which joins all the centres of circular turns, called axis of helix.

(a) Radius of helical path : $r=\frac{m v \sin \theta}{q B} \quad \text{ OR } \quad  r=\frac{m V_{\perp}}{q B}$

(b) Time period : $\mathrm{T}=\frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}}$

(c) Pitch of helix :The linear distance travelled by the charge particle in one revolution or in one time period along external magnetic field direction is called 'pitch of helix'.

$\mathrm{p}=(\mathrm{v} \cos \theta) \mathrm{T}$

$\text { where } \mathrm{T}=\displaystyle \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{~m}}{\mathrm{qB}} \Rightarrow \mathrm{p}=\displaystyle \frac{2 \pi \mathrm{mv} \cos \theta}{\mathrm{qB}}$

$$Lorentz Force: When a charge is moving in a region, where both electric field E and magnetic field B exist, then electric and magnetic forces are acting on it. The resultant of these forces called electromagnetic or Lorentz force on charge. (zero gravity).

Net Electromagnetic force is known as Lorentz force.

blocks.text:
Current Carrying wire in Uniform Magnetic Field : When a current carrying conductor placed in magnetic field, a magnetic force exerts on each free electron which are present inside the conductor. The resultant of these forces on all the free electrons is called magnetic force on conductor.

Net force on wire due to all such current elements

$\vec{F}=I(\vec{l} \times \vec{B})$

If B is uniform,

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{F}}=\mathrm{I}\left(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~L}}_{\mathrm{eff}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}\right)$

$L_{\text {eff }}$ is the displacement vector from starting point of current to end point of current.

Direction of magnetic force :

Magnetic force on the wire we can find by Right Hand Palm Rule

Magnetic Force Between Two Parallel Current Carrying Wires :

Definition of Ampere

Magnetic force/unit length for both infinite length conductor gives as

$\mathrm{f}=\dfrac{\mu_0 \mathrm{I}_1 \mathrm{I}_2}{2 \pi \mathrm{~d}}=\dfrac{\left(4 \pi \times 10^{-7}\right)(1)(1)}{2 \pi(1)}=2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$

'Ampere' is the current which, when passed through each of two parallel infinite long straight conductors placed in free space at a distance of 1 m from each other, produces between them a force  $2 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~N} / \mathrm{m}$.

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Torque on a Magnetic Dipole in Uniform Magnetic Field:

(a) Bar magnet

Consider a bar magnet of magnetic moment  $\vec{M}$  held in a uniform magnetic field $\vec(B)$ making an angle  $\theta$ with the field. Then the magnet experiences a torque given by

Torque = force × perpendicular distance between force couple

$\begin{aligned} \tau & =\mathrm{MB} \sin \theta, \text { where } \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{m} \ell \\ \vec{\tau} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \end{aligned}$

$\tau=\mathrm{MB} \sin \theta$

(b) Coil or Loop : If a loop carries a current of magnitude $I$ and magnetic moment $\vec{M}$ held in a uniform magnetic field $\vec{B}$ making an angle $\theta$

Then the loop experiences a torque given by,

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}  \end{aligned}$

If loop have N turns then

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\mathrm{NI}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{~A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ \tau & =\mathrm{NIAB} \sin \theta \end{aligned} \quad  \text { where } \vec{M}=N I \vec{A}$

Note:

• Tendency of torque on dipole is try to align the $\vec{M}$ in the direction of  $\vec{B}$ or tries to makes the axis of dipole parallel to $\vec{B}$ or makes the plane of coil (or loop) perpendicular to $\vec{B}$.

Work Done in Rotating the Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field:

When a bar magnet or coil of dipole moment M is kept in a uniform magnetic field B it experiences a torque which tries to align it in the direction of external magnetic field B . Work has to be done in rotation the magnet or coil.

$\begin{aligned}  & \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{MB}\left(\cos \theta_1-\cos \theta_2\right) \end{aligned}$

Potential Energy of the Coil in Uniform Magnetic Field: The potential energy of dipole defined as work done in rotating the dipole from a direction perpendicular to the given direction.

$\text { Work done in rotating the dipole from } \theta_1=90^{\circ} \text { to } \theta_2=0^{\circ}$

$\begin{aligned} &$$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}=\mathrm{MB}\left(\cos 90^{\circ}-\cos \theta\right) \\ & \mathrm{U}=-\mathrm{MB} \cos \theta \end{aligned}$$\\ &\text { In vector form } U=-\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}} \cdot \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}} \end{aligned}$$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Moving Coil Galvanometer:

Construction: The galvanometer consists of a coil, with many turns, free to rotate about a fixed axis, in a uniform radial magnetic field. There is a cylindrical soft iron core which not only makes the field radial but also increases the strength of the magnetic field. A spiral spring is also attached to the coil which resists the rotation of coil.

Working Principle: When a current carrying coil is placed in a magnetic field, it experiences a torque

$\begin{aligned} \vec{\tau} & =\operatorname{NI}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{A}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}) \\ \tau & =\operatorname{NIAB} \sin \theta \\ \tau & =\operatorname{NIAB} \end{aligned}$

$\left(\theta=90^{\circ} \text { due to radial magnetic field }\right)$

This torque tends to rotate the coil by $ \phi$ angle.

The spring S provides a counter torque $ \mathrm{C} \phi$ that balances the magnetic torque. In equilibrium,

$\mathrm{C} \phi=\mathrm{NIAB} \Rightarrow \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{C}}{\mathrm{NAB}} \phi$

$I \propto \phi$

Current Sensitivity: Current sensitivity is defined as the deflection produced in the galvanometer when a unit current flows through it.

$\text { C.S. }=\frac{\phi}{I}=\frac{N A B}{C}(\operatorname{rad} / A) $

Voltage Sensitivity :Voltage sensitivity is equal to the deflection per unit voltage applied across the voltmeter.

$\text { V.S. }=\frac{\phi}{V}=\frac{\phi}{I R}=\frac{N A B}{C R}(\mathrm{rad} / \mathrm{V})$

Atomic Magnetism: Consider an electron revolving around a nucleus in an atom. Due to the motion of the electrons, the orbit behaves like a current-carrying loop. Due to this, the magnetic field is produced at the centre of the orbit. This is called 'atomic magnetism'.

(a) Effective current

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{q}}{\mathrm{~T}}=\frac{\mathrm{e}}{\mathrm{~T}}=\mathrm{ef}=\frac{\mathrm{e} \omega}{2 \pi}=\frac{\mathrm{ev}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \\ & \mathrm{I}=\frac{\mathrm{qv}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}} \text { (In general) } \end{aligned}$

(b) Induced Magnetic Field at the center

$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{B}_{\text{in}} &= \frac{\mu_0 I}{2 r} = \frac{\mu_0 e}{2 T r} = \frac{\mu_0 e f}{2 r} = \frac{\mu_0}{2 r} \left( \frac{e v}{2 \pi r} \right) \\ &= \frac{\mu_0 e v}{4 \pi r^2} \\ \mathrm{B}_{\text{in}} &= \frac{\mu_0 q v}{4 \pi r^2} \quad \text{(In general)} \end{aligned}$

(c) Magnetic Moment

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{M}=\mathrm{IA}=\left(\frac{\mathrm{ev}}{2 \pi \mathrm{r}}\right) \pi \mathrm{r}^2=\frac{\mathrm{e} \omega \mathrm{r}^2}{2}=\frac{\mathrm{evr}}{2} \\ & \mathrm{M}=\frac{\mathrm{qvr}}{2}(\text { In general }) \end{aligned}$

NOTE: The ratio of magnetic moment to angular momentum, called the gyromagnetic ratio of a uniform rotating object which is charged uniformly, is always a constant and equal to half of the specific charge. Irrespective of the shape of the conductor M/L=q/2m

The magnetic field at axial point (or End-on position) of dipole:  $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{2 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{r}^3}$

The magnetic field at equatorial position (Broad-side on position) of dipole:  $\vec{B}=\frac{\mu_0}{4 \pi} \frac{(-\vec{M})}{r^3}$

Angular SHM of magnetic dipole:

When a dipole is suspended in a uniform magnetic field it will align itself parallel to field. Now if it is given a small angular displacement $\theta$ with respect to its equilibrium position. The restoring torque acts on it :

$\mathrm{T}=2 \pi \sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{MB}}} \quad \text { where } \mathrm{I}: \text { Moment of Inertia }=\frac{\mathrm{ml}^2}{12}\{\mathrm{~m} \text { : mass of magnet, } \ell: \text { length of magnet }\}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Magnetizing field or Magnetic Intensity (H) : Field in which a material is placed for magnetization, called as magnetizing field.

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{o}}} \\ & \text { unit of } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}}: \mathrm{A} / \mathrm{m} \\ & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{~B}}_{\mathrm{o}}: \text { Magnetic Field } \\ & \mu_0: \text { Permeability of free space } \end{aligned}$

$\text { Intensity of magnetization ( } \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}} \text { ) }$: When a magnetic material is placed in magnetising field then induced dipole moment per unit volume of that material is known as intensity of magnetisation.

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{M}}}{\mathrm{~V}}$

$\text { unit of } \vec{I}: A / m \quad\left\{\because \frac{\vec{M}}{V}=\frac{I \vec{A}}{V}=\frac{\text { ampere } \times \text { meter }^2}{\text { meter }^3}\right\}$

Induced magnetic field due to these induced dipoles in the material is given by:

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mu_{\mathrm{o}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}$

Magnetic susceptibility  $\left(\chi_m\right)$ :

$\chi_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{H}}$ [It is a scalar with no units & dimensions].

Physically it represents the ease with which a magnetic material can be magnetised.

Note: A material with more $\chi_{\mathrm{m}}$ can be changed into a magnet easily.

Magnetic Permeability $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ :

It represents the degree up to which a material can be penetrated by the magnetic field lines.

$\text { Relative Permeability ( } \mu_r \text { ) }$:

$\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0}$

It has no units and dimensions.

$\text { Relation between } \mu \text { and } \chi_{\mathrm{m}}$ :

When a magnetic material is placed in a magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}$  for magnetization, then total magnetic field in the material is

$\begin{aligned} & \mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\left(1+\chi_{\mathrm{m}}\right) \end{aligned}$

For vacuum, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0$

For air, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1.04, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0.04$

Magnetic Hysteresis: Only Ferromagnetic materials show magnetic hysteresis, when Ferromagnetic material is placed in external magnetic field for magnetization.

  • Magnetizing Field Increase: As the magnetizing field increases, the magnetic field inside the material also increases.
  • Saturation: At a certain point, further increase in the magnetizing field causes no change in the magnetic field inside (saturation).
  • Decrease in Magnetizing Field: When the magnetizing field is reduced, the magnetic field inside decreases (A to B).
  • Retentivity: After removing the magnetizing field, a residual magnetic field remains in the material $\text { (known as Retentivity, } B_r \text { ). }$
  • Coercivity: To remove the residual magnetic field, an external field is applied in the opposite direction until the net magnetic field is zero (B to C). The field strength required to do this is called Coercivity $\left(H_c\right)$
  • Reversal of Magnetization: As the magnetizing field is increased further, the magnetic field inside the material starts rising again (C to D).
  • Cycle Repeats: The curve repeats as the magnetizing field is decreased and reversed, showing hysteresis (lagging of B behind H).
  • Hysteresis Curve: The lag of B behind H forms the hysteresis curve.
Cause of hysteresis: By removing external magnetizing field (H = 0), the magnetic moment of some domains remains aligned in the applied direction of previous magnetizing field which results into a residual magnetism.

Hysteresis Loss:

• The area of the hysteresis loop is equal to the energy loss per cycle per unit volume.
    • Its value is different for different materials.
    • The work done per cycle per unit volume of material is equal to the area of the hysteresis loop.

$\text { Total energy loss in material }=\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}$

$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\text { volume of material } \times \text { area of hysteresis curve } \times \text { frequency } \times \text { time. }$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t} \text { joule } \\ & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{~J}} \text { calorie } \end{aligned}$

Induced magnetic field due to these induced dipoles in the material is given by:

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mu_{\mathrm{o}} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}}$

Magnetic susceptibility  $\left(\chi_m\right)$ :

$\chi_{\mathrm{m}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{H}}$ [It is a scalar with no units & dimensions].

Magnetic Permeability $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ :

$\mu=\frac{\mathrm{B}}{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\text { Total magnetic field inside a material }}{\text { Magnetizing field }}$

$Unit of  \mu: \mu=\dfrac{B_m}{H} \equiv \dfrac{W b / m^2}{A / m}=\dfrac{\text { Weber }}{A-m}=\dfrac{H-A}{A-m}=\dfrac{H}{m}$

$\text { Relative Permeability ( } \mu_r \text { ) }$:

$\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\dfrac{\mu}{\mu_0}$

$\text { Relation between } \mu \text { and } \chi_{\mathrm{m}}$ :

When a magnetic material is placed in a magnetic field $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}$  for magnetization, then total magnetic field in the material is

$\begin{aligned} & \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{m}}=\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{o}}+\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\text {in }}\left\{\overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\text {in }}=\text { induced field. }\right\} \\ & \because \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_0=\mu_0 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{H}}^{;} ; \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}_{\mathrm{in}}=\mu_0 \overrightarrow{\mathrm{I}} \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \therefore \vec{B}_m=\mu_o(\vec{H}+\vec{I}) \\ & B_m=\mu_o(H+I) \\ & \mu H=\mu_0 H\left(1+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{H}\right) \end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned} & \mu=\mu_{\mathrm{o}}\left(1+\chi_{\mathrm{m}}\right) \\ & \frac{\mu}{\mu_{\mathrm{o}}}=\left(1+\chi_{\mathrm{m}}\right) \\ & \mu_{\mathrm{r}}=\left(1+\chi_{\mathrm{m}}\right) \end{aligned}$

For vacuum, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0$

For air, $\mu_{\mathrm{r}}=1.04, \chi_{\mathrm{m}}=0.04$

Hysteresis Loss:

$\text { Total energy loss in material }=\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}$

$\mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\text { volume of material } \times \text { area of hysteresis curve } \times \text { frequency } \times \text { time. }$

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t} \text { joule } \\ & \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{H}}=\frac{\mathrm{V} \times \mathrm{A} \times \mathrm{n} \times \mathrm{t}}{\mathrm{~J}} \text { calorie } \end{aligned}$
